title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (adult)
subject: surgery-trauma
summary: Give one IV dose of the right agent (usually cefazolin 2 g, 3 g if 120 kg or more) within 60 minutes before incision (120 minutes for vancomycin and fluoroquinolones), redose for long operations or blood loss over 1500 mL, and stop within 24 hours.

sections.title: When prophylaxis is indicated
items: Clean-contaminated procedures (entry into the gut, biliary, respiratory, genital or urinary tract) and clean procedures with an implant or where infection would be disastrous (cardiac, joint replacement, vascular graft, neurosurgery).
Not needed for clean procedures without implants such as clean orthopaedic surgery without hardware, or low-risk elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Contaminated or dirty surgery (perforated viscus, established infection, open fracture) needs a treatment course, not prophylaxis.
Target the likely flora: staphylococci and streptococci for clean surgery; add gram-negative and anaerobic cover for colorectal, appendix, mucosal head and neck, and gynaecological surgery.

sections.title: Timing and dose
items: Start the dose within 60 minutes before incision; start vancomycin and fluoroquinolones within 120 minutes because of long infusion times (ASHP 2013). WHO accepts administration within 120 minutes before incision; ASHP timing is followed here.
Cefazolin 2 g IV for most adults, 3 g if weight is 120 kg or more; children 30 mg/kg (not above the adult dose).
If a limb tourniquet is used, finish the infusion before inflation.
Caesarean delivery: give before skin incision, not after cord clamping.

sections.title: Redosing and duration
items: Redose when the operation lasts longer than 2 half-lives of the drug or blood loss exceeds 1500 mL, counting from the start of the first dose: cefazolin and cefuroxime every 4 hours, cefoxitin every 2 hours, clindamycin every 6 hours. No intraoperative redosing is needed for vancomycin, metronidazole or gentamicin.
Stop within 24 hours; a single dose is enough for most procedures. WHO recommends against continuing prophylaxis after the operation ends.
Do not continue antibiotics because drains, urinary catheters or central lines remain in place.
Gentamicin in obesity (more than 20% above ideal body weight): dose on ideal body weight plus 40% of the difference between actual and ideal weight.

sections.title: Beta-lactam allergy
items: Clarify the reaction: many penicillin allergy labels are not true IgE-mediated allergy, and cefazolin is usually tolerated after non-severe, non-IgE reactions.
Severe or IgE-mediated reaction (anaphylaxis, angioedema, severe cutaneous reaction): clindamycin 900 mg IV or vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV for clean procedures.
When gram-negative cover is needed, add gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV single dose, aztreonam, or a fluoroquinolone to clindamycin or vancomycin.
Colorectal and appendix surgery with severe allergy: clindamycin plus gentamicin (or aztreonam or a fluoroquinolone), or metronidazole plus gentamicin or a fluoroquinolone.

sections.title: Procedure-specific first choice (ASHP 2013)
items: Cefazolin: cardiac, vascular, neurosurgery, hernia repair, breast, joint replacement, hip fracture fixation, gastroduodenal surgery, caesarean delivery, hysterectomy.
High-risk laparoscopic or open biliary surgery: cefazolin (alternatives cefoxitin, ceftriaxone or ampicillin-sulbactam).
Uncomplicated appendicectomy: cefazolin plus metronidazole, or cefoxitin.

Colorectal: cefazolin plus metronidazole, cefoxitin, ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, ampicillin-sulbactam or ertapenem; for elective colorectal surgery also give oral antibiotics with mechanical bowel preparation (WHO).
Clean-contaminated head and neck: cefazolin or cefuroxime plus metronidazole, or ampicillin-sulbactam.
Urological procedures: choice depends on the procedure and the urine culture; treat bacteriuria before elective urological surgery.
Known MRSA colonisation before cardiac or implant surgery: add vancomycin 15 mg/kg to cefazolin.

sections.title: Other surgical site infection measures (WHO)
items: Do not remove hair routinely; if essential, use clippers, never a razor.
Use alcohol-based chlorhexidine for surgical skin preparation.
Decolonise known Staphylococcus aureus nasal carriers with mupirocin 2% nasal ointment, with or without chlorhexidine body wash, before cardiothoracic and orthopaedic surgery.
Maintain normothermia and perioperative glucose control, including in patients without diabetes.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving the dose after incision, or more than 60 minutes before it (120 minutes for vancomycin).
Continuing prophylaxis for several days (for example repeated ceftriaxone doses, a common practice in India) instead of a single dose; this drives resistance without reducing infection.
Forgetting to redose in long operations or after major blood loss.
Using vancomycin routinely in place of cefazolin: it is less effective against methicillin-sensitive S. aureus and gives no gram-negative cover.
Underdosing obese patients.

drugs.name: Cefazolin
drugs.dose: 2 g IV (3 g if 120 kg or more); children 30 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)

drugs.name: Cefuroxime
drugs.dose: 1.5 g IV; children 50 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)

drugs.name: Cefoxitin
drugs.dose: 2 g IV; children 40 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)

drugs.name: Clindamycin
drugs.dose: 900 mg IV; children 10 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)
drugs.notes: Redose every 6 hours. Beta-lactam allergy alternative.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg IV infused over at least 60 minutes, starting within 120 minutes before incision; children 15 mg/kg
drugs.notes: No intraoperative redosing. Reserve for MRSA colonisation or severe beta-lactam allergy.

drugs.name: Gentamicin
drugs.dose: 5 mg/kg IV single dose; children 2.5 mg/kg
drugs.notes: Use adjusted weight in obesity; avoid repeated doses in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.dose: 500 mg IV; children 15 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)
drugs.notes: Anaerobic cover for colorectal, appendix, head and neck and gynaecological surgery.

drugs.name: Ertapenem
drugs.dose: 1 g IV single dose; children 15 mg/kg (maximum adult dose)
drugs.notes: Colorectal option; avoid routine use where carbapenem resistance is a concern.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: Biliary surgery, or colorectal with metronidazole.
